letters.name: a
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'a' in English 'cat' — short and open. In some words it sounds like 'ah' as in 'father'.

letters.name: b
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'b' but softer — Danish 'b' has less puff of air. Touch your lips together lightly.

letters.name: c
letters.memoryTrick: Mostly appears in loanwords. Before e/i/y it's usually /s/ like 's' in 'see'; otherwise /k/ like 'c' in 'cat'.

letters.name: d
letters.memoryTrick: At the start of a word it's like English 'd'. After a vowel it becomes the famous Danish 'soft d' — place your tongue tip behind your bottom teeth and say a buzzing 'th' like in 'the'.

letters.name: e
letters.memoryTrick: Can be like 'e' in English 'bed' or more closed like 'ay' in 'say' without the glide. At the end of words it's often a schwa like 'a' in 'about'.

letters.name: f
letters.memoryTrick: Just like English 'f' — top teeth on bottom lip and blow air. Same sound in 'far' (father) in both Danish and English.

letters.name: g
letters.memoryTrick: At the start of a word it's like English 'g' in 'go'. After a vowel it often softens or becomes silent — 'dag' (day) sounds like 'dah'.

letters.name: h
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'h' in 'hat' — but watch out: it's SILENT before 'j' and 'v'! So 'hjerte' (heart) starts with a 'y' sound, and 'hvad' (what) starts with 'v'.

letters.name: i
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'ee' in English 'see' but shorter and more tense. Also the Danish word 'i' means 'in' — a very common preposition!

letters.name: j
letters.memoryTrick: Always like English 'y' in 'yes', never like English 'j'. So 'Jul' (Christmas) sounds like 'Yool'. Think: J = Y in Danish.

letters.name: k
letters.memoryTrick: At the start of a word it's aspirated — a strong burst of air like 'k' in English 'kite'. After 's' (sk-) it loses the puff and is softer.

letters.name: l
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'l' in 'light'. Danish 'l' is always clear and light — never dark like the 'l' in English 'full'.

letters.name: m
letters.memoryTrick: Just like English 'm' — press your lips together and hum. 'Mor' (mother) is one of the first words Danish children learn.

letters.name: n
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'n' in 'no'. Tongue tip against the roof of your mouth just behind the teeth.

letters.name: o
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'o' in English 'go' but shorter and without the glide. 'Og' (and) is one of the most common Danish words — it sounds like 'ow'.

letters.name: p
letters.memoryTrick: At the start of a word it's strongly aspirated — like English 'p' in 'pin' with a big puff of air. After 's' it loses the puff, like in 'spise' (eat).

letters.name: q
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords and always followed by 'u'. Sounds just like 'k'. Think of 'quiz' — same in both languages!

letters.name: r
letters.memoryTrick: This is the classic Danish guttural R — made in the back of the throat like a soft gargle, similar to the French 'r'. Don't roll it!

letters.name: s
letters.memoryTrick: Always unvoiced like 's' in English 'see' — never voiced like 'z'. Danish has no 'z' sound for 's', ever.

letters.name: t
letters.memoryTrick: Strongly aspirated like English 't' in 'time'. After 's' it loses the puff — 'stor' (big) has a softer t.

letters.name: u
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'oo' in English 'boot' but with more rounded lips and slightly shorter. Danish 'u' is much more rounded than English 'u'.

letters.name: v
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'v' but with less friction — the bottom lip barely touches the top teeth. Think 'soft v'. The Danish word 'vand' (water) sounds like 'van'.

letters.name: w
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords and sounds like Danish 'v'. 'Weekend' is the same word in both languages — just pronounced with a Danish accent!

letters.name: x
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords. Sounds like 'ks' as in English 'box'. 'Xylofon' (xylophone) is one of very few Danish words starting with x.

letters.name: y
letters.memoryTrick: Like German 'ü' or French 'u' — purse your lips as if to say 'oo' but try to say 'ee' instead. It's a front rounded vowel. 'Yndig' (lovely) is a great practice word.

letters.name: z
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords and almost always sounds like 's', not like English 'z'. 'Zebra' is the same word in Danish and English — but the 'z' sounds like 's'.

letters.name: ae
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'e' in English 'bed' but slightly more open. It's the sound you make when you open your mouth for the dentist! 'Æble' (apple) is the perfect word to remember this letter — it even looks like an apple with a stem.

letters.name: oe
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'eu' in French 'deux' or German 'ö'. Round your lips as if to say 'oh' but try to say 'eh' instead. 'Øl' (beer) is every Dane's favorite word — remember it by thinking of a crossed-out O as a 'no' to water, meaning beer!

letters.name: aa
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'o' in English 'born' or 'aw' in 'saw'. It's the last letter of the Danish alphabet, added in 1948. 'År' (year) is a great first word — think of it as 'aw-r' and remember that å looks like an 'a' wearing a little halo.
